BasePK: 3822401

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, when Dr. Carolyn Kerrigan did a study for the department last year, one of the things she said was this:
There is an urgent need for controlled experimental studies of breast implants to address countless issues regarding their usage. Mandatory information concerning implant composition, degradation, excretion, placement, contracture, infection and others must be determined on a clinically applicable animal model.
The FDA in the United States is doing continuing research with regard to all implants. We are also paying for work to be done in Canada as well.
We will undertake to make every possible effort to ensure that any implant, whether breast implants or other surgical devices, is safe and efficacious before being implanted in Canadians.

You are a research assistant analysing speeches from the Canadian House of Commons, 1953-1993.

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.
2. `procedural_score`: a number from 0 to 1 indicating how far the speech moves away from substantive policy discussion toward procedural, partisan, dilatory, or purely formal parliamentary language.

Topic rules:
- Be specific: "old-age pensions" not "social policy"; "railway freight rates" not "transportation".
- Lower-case unless a proper noun requires capitalisation.
- Ignore routine openings such as "Mr. Speaker".
- If substantive content is present, label the substantive topic.
- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

Score rule:
- 0 = almost entirely substantive policy, administration, legislation, public spending, economic/social issues, or government action.
- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.
- 1 = almost entirely procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal, with little substantive policy content.

Procedural, partisan, dilatory, or formal content includes points of order, privilege, Speaker rulings, adjournment, closure, time allocation, order of business, committee or bill-stage mechanics, divisions, standing orders, unanimous consent, tabling, leave of the House, short formal interventions, repeated objections, delay tactics, or speeches mainly criticising parties, governments, oppositions, leaders, or electoral records instead of developing a policy argument.

When in doubt, give a lower score if the speech contains meaningful substantive policy discussion.

BasePK: 3822457

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, if we go back to my argument before, if a bill is introduced in this House to reduce Mr. Jones' salary from $50,000 to $25,000, the charge has been reduced. I am suggesting to Your Honour that a private member, I or any member of the opposition, or any back-bench member of the government, could move an amendment to that bill to increase the amount to $40,000. As long as it was within the original amount, then it could be increased.
What I am saying in this case, Your Honour, is that in each of the amendments to which the government House leader objects, the other place has provided for amendments that will increase the amount to something less than they were before, but not more than they were before.

BasePK: 3822510

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed very pleased to address this motion, a motion to consider special initiatives for aboriginal youth.
I am pleased because aboriginal youth and the development of positive programs have been a personal interest and involvement of mine for many years. This is a matter of tremendous importance, as other members have previously stated.
The needs regarding employment, education and health are all interrelated and should be considered together, although separately each deserves its own consideration.
Without education it is very difficult to obtain employment and without health it is very difficult to obtain an education or employment. With education and employment it is much easier to stay healthy. So the needs, if and when properly addressed, will result in aboriginal youth who are, among other positives, proud of who they are. Aboriginal youth will feel a part of this country once again, to the extent that they then can become positive contributors as nation builders in every aspect.
The problems we have come to know too well are immense but not insurmountable. I think aboriginal youth want to contribute. Given the same chance as everyone else they can become winners like everyone else. First they have to feel good. They have to feel good about who they are and where they are going, but collectively we must first deal with myths and stereotypes that have been proliferated over the years. The days of the no good, lazy, drunken Indian must come to an end. How does it happen? One of the ways is with education. Another is with employment.
When dealing with aboriginal youth I am often asked: "How is it that you have the highest suicide rates, the highest unemployment rates, the highest drop-out rates from high school, the highest inmate population rates in jails"? In yesterday's edition of The Globe and Mail these kinds of statistics continued to appear. Let me quote from the article:
The statistics compiled by the Canadian Institute of Child Health on suicide among people from the ages of 15 to 19 go beyond the basic question of why anyone to whom the full flavour of life should just be dawning would wish to end it. Why would young people in Canada's north be apparently so much readier than others to quit this life? Is it linked in some way to the relative hostility of their environment? The despair that feeds on unemployment and low incomes? Is this the lot of a culture tom between the old ways and new ways, seduced nightly by the dish-antenna visions of southern lifestyles and escape through the

April 5, 1990
Private Members' Business
bottle? Is it the inevitable fate of a huge territory of scattered communities?
Whatever the explanation-and it might be a hellish alchemy compounded from all of the above-it is clear that the native northerner can count substantially fewer of the blessings of life than other Canadians. Fewer in almost any category you care to mention.
The unemployment rate among native northerners, reports the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs, is among the highest in Canada, reaching 50 per cent in some communities-
I might add that in some areas it is as high as 85 per cent. It continues:
The Northwest Territories has the highest per capita incidence of alcohol offences in Canada, and probably a very high rate of substance abuse.
Although the article refers to the north, I do not think it is very much different in other parts of Canada. In fact at home the suicide rate is even higher. Where the article mentions rates four to five times the national average, ours have been as high as ten to twelve times.
I think over time, with self-fulfilling prophecies, much of this has happened because we as native people have become to believe that we are no good or lazy or that you have to drink to be an Indian or that we should die before a certain age.
Much can happen to change the world for aboriginal youth. Much has been done in the past. Allow me to thank all of those concerned for their efforts to date, but much more needs to be done. This motion, when passed, would begin that process. When the motion was first introduced I wanted to refer to a couple of noteworthy events related to the issue. I think they are still relevant.
First, after 10 years of negotiations, the UN General Assembly unanimously adopted the first convention on the rights of the child. I applaud the members involved whole-heartedly. Then during the same week the Leader of the NDP in his final speech to this House spoke very eloquently on the plight of the poor and in particular of children in our affluent society of Canada. Yet, for the children who are referred to throughout those speeches and documents, many of those are aboriginal children.
In 1990, in Canada, we still have aboriginal youth who go to school every morning hungry or too hungry to concentrate or to study or to do their homework. Until the employment, education and health needs are addressed and met, we will have this cycle of desperation.
What can be done? I do not want to appear totally negative because there are many success stories. Aboriginal youth want to contribute. In fact I believe aboriginal peoples want to contribute. We want to contribute to the development of our own youth. We know they will then become strong segments of Canadian society and, in that way, we will then have a stronger Canada.
A basic minimum to accomplish this is for full, meaningful consultation to occur with aboriginal peoples. If I may mention a personal bias, I believe that personal, physical, mental and spiritual development must first happen as a foundation. Sir, when you were the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, you contributed to that positive development. I thank you for that, but I think you will also agree that it was because you consulted aboriginal people yourself that made those sport programs successful. I was grateful, therefore, for the announcement by our colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and N [...truncated]

BasePK: 3822531

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words today concerning women's centres in relation to comments that the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands has made.
Some 10 years ago in Scarborough we set up a women's centre. I was a member of the board founding that centre. It was very important to establish the centre in order to reach out to women who are having difficulty so that we could as sisters help them. In the process of setting up that women's centre we looked for funds. We spent a lot of time around the table filling in those applications, getting the right words in order that the funding would become available, but at no time did we believe 10 years ago that our sole funding for women's centres was to be from the federal government.
At that time we were looking to foundations, to the community, and to fund raising events to see how we could have funding from various levels. I am very pleased today, thanks to two very wonderful individuals in Scarborough, Nina Willcocks and Linda Davis, who have diversified this funding so that now there is very little funding from various levels of government in order to provide services for social justice and economic equality for the women in Scarborough.

April 6, 1990
Supply
I have a question and comment. The hon. member speaks about funding cuts. Let us look at some of the numbers. In 1984-85, the year just before the Conservative Party took over the government, the funding was about $8 million for women's programs under Secretary of State. There has been a tremendous increase in that funding. In 1988-89 it was $13 million.
The commitment demonstrated by a number of women within our own party in order to increase funding dramatically over the last six years is a great credit to the government and these women. Many have benefited from those programs.
I think that it is time that we started setting some of the record straight in terms of the advantages we have been able to provide for /omen, such as jobs and the number of women who have been able to establish their own businesses. Two-thirds of the businesses in Canada started in the last six years have been started by women.
I wanted to set the record straight. I look forward to doing so as we progress through this debate.

BasePK: 3822608

Speech:
Madam Speaker, April 7 is World Health Day. This year the theme is "Health and the Environment".
Recent environmental disasters such as the Hagers-ville tire fire emphasize the need for all countries to examine and begin to address the environmental hazards that may pose continuing health problems for future generations of Canadians.
Canada is in an enviable position with its high standard of living, its excellent health and social services system and its incredible supply of natural resources. But we all know that no country can afford to be complacent. We must work hard to preserve what we have and ensure that our environment is a positive force for healthy living.
I would urge you all, both as individual Canadians and as members in your own communities, to think globally and act locally, and to urge your friends, your families and your constituents to do the same.

BasePK: 3822614

Speech:
Madam Speaker, tourism is the largest growing business in Canada, and this government is set on a course to destroy it.
Since 1984, the size and capabilities of the federal Department of Tourism have been steadily reduced by 75 per cent. The cuts to VIA Rail will effectively keep people from visiting many parts of this country. This all comes at a time when support for the industry should be
increasing in order to accommodate the world-wide rapid growth of tourism.
But most devastating of all is the proposed goods and services tax with its ill-conceived rebate which will be an absolute nuisance to travellers.
We have heard nothing but complaints from tour operators over this tax. As a result of an across-the-board 7 per cent sales tax on such items as hotel rooms, attractions and motor coach charters, many tour companies will no longer be able to market Canada as an affordable destination. A loss of tourist revenue translates into a loss of jobs.
I urge the government to stop this assault on the tourist industry by scrapping this tax and doing something for this country.

BasePK: 3822616

Speech:
Madam Speaker, on Saturday, Canadians can vote for or against the goods and services tax in malls and public places throughout Canada. On Monday, they can vote at their workplace. I suspect they are going to vote against it; at least the opportunity is there.
But what about Parliament Hill? We in the NDP have set up a balloting station here on the Hill. To be specific, it will open on Monday at 10 a.m. in the Commonwealth Room right here in the Centre Block. We are inviting staff, visitors on the Hill and MPs to vote.
As a matter of fact, I would like to specifically invite the Tory MPs, the back-benchers, to come and vote on Monday at ten o'clock. It is a secret ballot. I know many of them would like to vote against the GST; here is an opportunity.

Core funding covers the kinds of expenses that keep these organizations open. In other words, it pays the rent, for lights, heat, incidentals of that nature and usually a part-time salary for a co-ordinator.
Project funding, as its name implies, covers a specific project put forward in a grant application by the organization to cover any number of things. It might have to do with studies relating to sexual assault victims. It might have to do with employment equity programs or shortterm education programs. Various and sundry projects come under project funding.

April 10, 1990

Speech:
Thke a look at the democratic institutions in this world and you will find that we are the longest winded legislature in the democratic free world. We sit more days, talking longer. There have only been two debates since 1950, at second reading, that have gone longer than two days in the British House of Commons. Debate went six days when they entered into the European Economic Community and three days when they got rid of the Greater London Council.
I had the opportunity of sitting on the opposition side for 12 years. I know how it used to be. The idea is to talk, talk, talk, to try to force the government to bring in closure or time allocation. I know it is a tactic which is used.
I really think that we in the House of Commons are on the edge of talking ourselves into irrelevancy. I think we should sit down and modernize what we are doing in this place. We should come in tune with the times. The member for Kingston and the Islands was talking of a week or two weeks for debate at second reading stage, yet they go for a maximum of two days in England on second reading.
There is lots of time. We are going to have another six hours of debate on this. There is going to be a chance for more discussion.
We really have to look at the fundamental way in which we run this place. Instead of always just opposing, getting counteracting ideas from the government side and then comments from the opposition, I think we should sit down and fundamentally look at how we run this place.
For example, I know the stall tactics of putting up petitions. In England every petition gets filed with the Clerk. They respond to them. We can file with the Clerk here. We do not have to stand up and spend hours of House of Commons time reading them. Nobody ever watches it on TV and nobody reports them in the paper. They are reported in the Order Paper when they are
April 24, 1990

filed so you get as much printed press as you do when you stand up and talk about them.
We can make some observations of how other Parliaments run their affairs. Instead of becoming irrelevant and wasting time, I think we should try and organize ourselves. Perhaps on an all-party basis the House Leaders would want to sit down to organize ourselves in a better way, instead of talking about such ridiculous stuff as jackboots.
You have to admit, when you get that sort of trash introduced as a speech in the House of Commons you have to question why we are standing here taking up time, why we are spending the money, why we are being so foolish.
So let us become a little more sensible and more realistic in the modern day. Let us use Parliament to debate matters and move on. We do not have to drag them out for a week or two weeks at a time. We have to move them along. I do not think we have to hear such trash as having two weeks debate on this, that and the other thing, or that it is a place of jackboots.
Closure and time allocation has been around for a long time. You can count the number of times the Liberals used it in the last Parliament before they turned the reins over to the Conservatives. They used it many times. We used it many times in the last Parliament. The pressures of the times are going to be realized. Nobody even comments on it any more in the press because it is used so regularly and they know it has to be, otherwise the opposition will just hold things up.
We saw what the NDP did on the goods and services tax. The very party which agreed with the goods and services tax in 1987 is now trying to talk it out at committee and in the House of Commons, through all kinds of procedural tactics, rather than getting on with it.
The government has the right to propose things. The House of Commons should dispose of things. The opposition may wish to oppose on certain occasions, it may wish to agree on certain occasions. If we oppose on all occasions and try to hold up the disposition of things for one week, two weeks, or three weeks, we become irrelevant here. I think we should look at the fundamen-

As you may be aware, Mr. Speaker, a number of post offices in rural Canada have been under attack for closing, conversion or the new expansion program of Canada Post. I must say that the advice and direction I am able to provide to these people comes down to one of just remaining vigilant, being constant and never giving up.
The Dubuc situation is one that provides us with a great deal of frustration and many of the other communities could find it very difficult to deal with. The community of Dubuc found itself 100 per cent in favour of maintaining service from the existing post office. Canada Post came into that community and asked if there was a business person who would be willing to provide service from his or her business location and establish a retail postal outlet in the community of Dubuc, Saskatchewan.
The people of Dubuc said no. None of the business people in the community of Dubuc wanted a retail postal outlet. They wanted service from the post office and a full-time postmaster working from that post office meeting the needs of that community. They even travelled to Ottawa to make their case before our committee, before the minister and before members of this House.
When Canada Post could not find a retail business that was willing to give service from a store, cafe, or even the grain elevator, Canada Post said: "All right. We will just close your post office and you will not get any service". Canada Post blackmailed the community, and now one of those businesses has said that it will put in a retail postal outlet, if it is the only way there can be service to the community and residents do not have to drive 15 miles to the next community to pick up registered mail, buy stamps, and those types of things.

Madam Speaker, I am privileged to have a chance to speak on Bill C-67 which, in a sense, is companion legislation to Bill C-66 which deals with concerns regarding diseases with animals.
We are now considering the matter of plant protection legislation to ensure that plant life in the agricultural sector, as well as in the forestry sector, will be protected from incoming pests, meaning insects or diseases. This means that we also control plant material leaving Canada in terms of ensuring that we are not infecting other parts of the world with pests or diseases that may have originated here.
Basically, we are trying to control or eliminate plant pests of one kind or another in the country. It is time that we deal with this issue. This is updated legislation. It replaces the Plant Quarantine Act that has been in obvious need of change for decades. This is an opportunity to do that.
I want to say at the outset that we in the New Democratic Party support this legislation. We feel that it is a good initiative. It will assist the agricultural community, as well as the forest industry, in making Canada more insect and disease free when it comes to the infestation of our plant life.

May 17, 1990
Government Orders
One of these areas concerns the incredible powers that are given to the Minister of Agriculture as well as agriculture officials. When you read the bill, Madam Speaker, you will notice that the Minister of Agriculture almost becomes a czar and is able to move in and deal quickly with an area that has been infected by insects, pests or diseases of one kind or another. It is good to have a disease SWAT team, a disease commando unit, to move in quickly to deal with a problem as early as possible. The earlier these issues are dealt with, the more chance there is to successfully eliminate them or deal with them.
However, we also realize that an over-zealous minister or an over-zealous official could cause problems. As my hon. friend who just spoke indicated, it would be appropriate and absolutely necessary to have at least draft regulations for the committee to consider at the same time that we are dealing with this legislation. Those regulations will lay out the parameters in terms of how the minister and agriculture officials will respond.
I also want to give some indication of a concern regarding the fees, charges and costs associated with the inspection, containment, quarantine initiatives and so on that will be taken. The bill indicates that in a sense we are attempting to introduce a cost-recovery initiative where the cost of a particular initiative, looking into a diseased plant area, would be borne largely by the producer.
I want to ask if that is reasonable. Is it not in all our interests as a society to ensure that our crops and our forest lands are disease free? At times, this would require an initiative on behalf of the producer to recognize that there appears to be a problem and we ought to deal with it. It may cost the producer his crop, or a portion of it.
If the entire cost of this analysis is being borne by the producer, there may at times be less than an immediate response to deal with this. We have seen and we are aware of instances in the past where producers have simply overlooked what was a problem, something which became a serious problem later. If we are going to encourage people to volunteer to deal with this, I think we should do so with some recognition that society as a whole will benefit and perhaps society as a whole should carry some of the costs.
I also want to say that I am pleased to see that the act grants authority to issue tickets, similar to traffic tickets, to violators of the act and the regulations that will be attached to it. I question that because Canadians expect protection. They expect a high level and a high degree of protection. They assume that the appropriate inspection processes are always being carried out. We know, unfortunately, that is not always the case.
When it comes to a country as susceptible as we are from time time to plant diseases coming in, it is important that we have a very high degree of inspection. That has been done extremely well by Agriculture Canada in the past. I would like to think that we will continue on with that tradition and not see this as an opportunity to simply privatize a number of first-class government services that we have known in the past. This is a question that we will obviously be pursuing at the committee stage.
On balance, we support the legislation. We are pleased that the government has brought it forward now. We look forward to dealing with it in committee and raising some of the appropriate concerns there. We again appeal to have as much of the regulations in place as possible for consideration when this bill gets to the committee stage.

It is an issue that I do not think anyone could have been elected to this House without addressing time and again in the various forums that led up to our election.
It is very obvious from the tone and tenor of the debate this afternoon on the amendments that everyone in the House recognizes how important this is. The debate is also being conducted in a manner in which I would like to see more of them conducted, with each member free to express his or her own point of view and to vote according to his or her own conscience or according to the wishes of his or her constituents.
Having said that, I do not know if very many of us are ready to handle the emotional weight that would be involved if we had to face many issues like this one.
The legislative committee that reviewed the bill deserves to be recognized and applauded for its work. It invested a tremendous amount of study and many hours in listening to witnesses and examining the same. It spent a lot of time in debate and in research. The members of the committee gave the issue much thought and did much soul-searching.
We all know that the bill was reported unamended. That does not mean that there was agreement, as we know. Far from it. This illustrates the problem that exists in trying to legislate a moral issue upon which there are greatly diverging views.
In my speech at second reading I said:
To achieve political solutions to the complex and controversial problems that come before us it is often necessary to accept compromise. On this issue, however, views are held so strongly and opinions are so galvanized that many of the people we represent are, because of personal convictions, unwilling or unable to compromise their position or their beliefs.
May 22, 1990

I went on to say:
Bill C-43 is by necessity a political answer to a moral question, and
as a political answer represents a compromise and moral values are
not subject to compromise.
My personal position is that life is sacred from the moment of conception until natural death. Many people who share that conviction with me have said that that they felt I compromised my views by supporting Bill C-43 at second reading. They asked how it was possible for me to accept a bill that was a compromise.
Politicians must face a reality that advocates outside of the legislative process do not have to face. We must sometimes accept a bill that is less than perfect when it is better than the alternative. At second reading the alternative was this bill or nothing. I supported it because it was better than the vacuum which existed, and which still exists. I supported it because it is still possible to strengthen it and provide more protection for the life of the unborn.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today to Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion.
When the Prime Minister indicated that his government would bring forward a bill on abortion during this session of Parliament, there was a collective sigh of relief across the country. That relief, however, was quickly shattered with the introduction of this bill. Bill C-43 completely fails to address the painful issue that is troubling this country's conscience.
I realize this is not a decision to be made lightly. I intend to vote against the bill in its present form. I believe this bill is a bad piece of legislation. Many of my constituents from the riding of Scarborough-Agincourt believe as I do, that human life begins at conception and must be protected by law at all stages of development.
Once we come to the unavoidable conclusion that the foetus is a human being, we must then come to the conclusion that this person must be given full protection of the law as would be given to any child in Canada today.
It is absolutely deplorable that anyone can say that a procedure which kills one human being for the convenience of another is a medical procedure. In simple terms, abortion is the killing of a human being and cannot be accepted. If we do not believe in life, then what can we believe in? Where is the value system? If we do not ensure that abortions are performed only to save the mother's life, then our society will be condoning abortion on demand.
I did not vote for Bill C-43 on second reading. Though I was disappointed that the bill reached committee stage, I hoped we would see some substantial amendments after the legislative committee had an opportunity to thoroughly examine the bill clause by clause. This was obviously not the case. I had hoped for an entirely different bill from the one we see before us today.

May 23, 1990
Government Orders
The abortion issue has not been rectified. The bill still does not recognize the fundamental value and dignity of each human being and the worth of each human life. I ask members of the House to consider the lives of unborn children above all else.
The only amendment that I can in conscience support is the one put forward by my colleague from Glengarry- Prescott-Russell which removes the word "health" from the bill. This would end any dubious claims of mental, emotional, fiscal or other reasons of so-called health which could be encompassed by such a broad definition.
This bill was flawed from the outset, and I dare say would not stand up constitutionally in a court of law. Therefore, it should not be before us at this time. It is obvious that the government, in choosing to put forward this bill at this particular time, decided it does not wish to deal with the real matter at hand, which is that of foetal rights.
The passage of this bill will lay open the door to medical experimentation upon the pre-born and would also leave open the question of usage of foetal tissue for dubious medical purposes.
I would also like to express my disappointment in the government's decision not to allow the free vote on this bill as was promised and expected.
I read in the paper today that some of my colleagues on the other side, members of cabinet, who are pro-life supporters will vote in favour of the bill. That saddens me. The constraints placed upon cabinet ministers to support this abortion bill is unconscionable.
I call upon all my colleagues in the House to give thought to why we are not addressing the real issues here today and to defeat this bill so that a comprehensive bill that looks at all the issues of foetal rights could be brought forward, or failing that, the rights of the unborn be placed where they rightfully belong, in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question. It is interesting for me particularly, because in the City of Victoria we have a program which has been noted right across the country in this precise area. That is a community policing program.
The City of Victoria Police Department, a few years ago, with the assistance of the Solicitor General's department, established a program of neighbourhood police stations which in a way is old hat. It is perhaps what the police used to do very well and it is taking that old idea and readapting into a modem urban setting.
Even in establishing the local police station there was a good deal of community consultation and preparation for that. Community committees were established and the community was asked to participate in the work of the neighbourhood police station. Much of the work was focused on the idea of the prevention of crime. I should add that there is also the need to deal with the prevention of the perception of crime. We now have five neighbourhood police stations in Victoria. So far all of them have appeared to be very successful in not only reducing the incidence of crime in the area, and particularly among young people, but also the perception of crime.
Surveys have shown that older people have the greatest fear that they may be subject to crime, and at the same time the surveys show that it is in fact young people who are the greatest victims of crime. Part of that is because crime in our urban society invariably happens at night, frequently associated with abuse of alcohol and drugs. It is quite a different pattern than one watches on television, and I think many of us get our images of crime as much from television and from the media as we do from the reality.
When one asks the police what is their busiest time of day, they will state that it is between 11 at night and four or five in the morning. Therefore, the work of the prevention of crime begins with the bringing into focus a real understanding of what crime is all about.

The government could do so much more than it has done in this area. Even in the United States, the federal government has shown greater leadership in trying to develop effective and sensible programs for the prevention of crime. Mr. Speaker, my remarks address the hon. member's question about why the government has not approved the proposal by the Ottawa-Carleton Economic Development Corporation for a new Ottawa-Chicago air service. As was stated in the House on February 19, by the former Minister of Transport, this government has been sensitive to the request but the proposal posed certain difficulties.
Air services between Canada and the United States are governed by bilateral air agreements, particularly the Main Air Services Agreement of 1966 which the member opposite mentioned, last revised in 1974. There is no provision in this agreement for an Ottawa-Chicago service. The inclusion of a provision for an Ottawa-Chicago service in the agreement would require that the agreement be amended to meet the requirements of the National Transportation Act. Amendments normally come about through govemment-to-govemment negotiations.

More importantly, Canada prefers a broadly-based pro-competitive approach that seeks to provide efficient air services to all our communities and opportunities for our air carrier industry. This cannot be achieved on the basis of piecemeal negotiations focusing exclusively on the needs of a single community.
When negotiations are undertaken with the United States, they will have to take an account of the national interest, including the aspirations of other Canadian cities that have made representations for improved services, and here I am thinking of Halifax, Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, to name but a few.
Let me assure you that Ottawa's request, along with those of other Canadian communities, has been given serious consideration. The government, however, is not prepared to take actions at this time on behalf of a single community which could jeopardize Canada's ability to pursue a broadly-based re-negotiation of the Canada- U.S. air relationship on terms favourable to Canada and to all interested communities.

June 15, 1990

that encourages most Canadians to support the free expression of ideas and the free distribution of photographic, audio-visual or other material.
The Criminal Code provides that using the mails to transmit obscene, indecent, immoral or scurrilous material constitutes an offence.

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I am in a little jam on this one. I agree with much of what the member has just said about gambling per se, but I find it difficult to support his motion. I guess what bothers me is that he was part of the government that brought in Lotto Canada and now he wants to restrict the advertising of it. I find that a bit of a contradiction, particularly since the member bringing this measure forward was Solicitor General for about four years between 1980 and 1984 and had ample opportunity at that time to bring forth the kind of measure that he is talking about now. He could have encouraged it in the cabinet at that time. Maybe he did and was not successful, I do not know.
I remember when Lotto Canada was introduced with fanfare. It was our belief that the federal government should not be in the gambling business. I remember that you had to be very well connected to the Liberal Party to get a franchise for selling Lotto Canada tickets. I remember most of all how a colleague of mine whose wife was contacted to be an agent for Lotto Canada. Somehow the communications had got mixed up in the Liberal Party and they thought that she was connected with the office of one of the Liberal members of Parliament. After she had been offered the franchise, they found out much to their chagrin that she was not the person they thought she was. She said "Well, that's fine. I don't really need it. I have an appointment with The Globe and Mail anyway." All of a sudden the franchise was forthcoming. That is the first thing I remember about Lotto Canada. The second thing I remember was the time that boxes of Lotto Canada tickets were missing.
When we formed the government in 1979 we were convinced that the federal government should not be in the lottery business in the first place. We divested ourselves of that under the leadership of the Right Hon. Joe Clark. We divested ourselves of that business because we did not believe that we should be doing it. We turned it over to the provinces for their administration and for their financial profit.
I do not hold to the lottery business at all. I have to say to the member, who was a member of the government at that time, since his government brought the lotto business into Canada, how did he expect the business to be propagated, by word of mouth? You know "Hey, pal, I've

June 18, 1990
Private Members' Business
got a ticket"? No, no. There was going to be advertising, and there was. If you will recall, there was heavy advertising on television of Lotto Canada tickets at the time. There was no hint that we should not be doing it at the time. Now we have it under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
This is what bothers me most of all about his motion, that at one time it was in the federal domain and there was nothing in the legislation at that time to restrict advertising of the lottery system. Now that it is in the provincial domain, we are supposed to restrict advertising for lotteries. I grant him that particularly lifestyle advertising is injurious and leads people to believe in some fantasies that are unhealthy, and that is not good. Ele has just cited the reason for bringing in the legislation tabled, and it happens to be Ontario advertising, and it could have been any other province as well, but has he made any overtures to the Government of Ontario, who are his soul mates? Has he asked it about the advertising it is doing so that it does not propagate what could become a disease, a fixation in advertising?
Once one introduces a measure like lotteries-I would rather that it would not be here-and then tells the provinces: "Here is what you cannot do with it," there is an element of paternalism that enters into it. I cannot believe that the provinces are going to be happy with any kind of instruction from the federal government about what is or what is not acceptable about the way they promote what we have already given them the right to promote.
I cannot believe that the provinces think they are so immature in the whole area of ethics, morality and promotion of this that they need guidance from the federal government on how guidelines ought to be set up for the promotion of this industry.
The hon. member's other point is that low income people tend to use their disposable income, of which they have a restricted amount, to buy lottery tickets that they may not be able to afford. This hurts them. If that is the pattern, I agree that it does. Would he then also suggest that, for example, if there is a higher percentage of cigarette smoking among low income people that there ought to be a diminished amount of advertising toward them, or that we ought to take fewer tax dollars from them? Should we increase the taxes for them?
Once one gets into a kind of socioeconomic grouping, I think one runs into trouble. I wonder about penny stocks. If there is ever an arena for gambling, it is in the whole area of penny stocks. Maybe that should be included. I guess the biggest problem that I have is the serious degree to which legislation like this could antagonize the provincial governments. I do not think we need that kind of confrontation in federal-provincial relations.
Now that we have an industry that I do not support and that I do not think is good, but which is entirely within the domain of the provinces, we ought to let the provinces do it and not try to pass legislation that instructs them in a kind of paternalistic way on how to conduct their activities.

June 18, 1990

to this clawback. It is widely opposed by seniors groups across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as you will recall, yesterday as I was supporting the government bill, Bill C-78, the proposed Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, the main thrust of my presentation related to the openness of the process and the significant steps that have been made in this bill to allow for public participation throughout the process. As I finished yesterday, I had just mentioned that as part of the bill there is a clause that has established a formal participant funding program to ensure that all stakeholders have the opportunity to participate in the mediation and public hearings that will occur under this bill.
Government Orders
This multi-million financial assistance program will open the environmental assessment process to Canadians who might not have had the financial resources to otherwise participate in public reviews.
This includes both opponents and proponents and applicants reflecting both sides of the issue will be equally considered for participant funding.
The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act even legislates the requirement that public comments aired in the environmental assessment must be considered before a decision is made on a major project. As well, public concerns must be reflected in mandatory study, mediation and panel reports.
The act also establishes the Canadian Environmental Assessment Agency. The new agency, which will be fully independent of all departments, including Environment Canada, has a mandate to examine and report on the implementation of the environmental assessment process across government. Each year the agency will be required to table in the House an annual report on this subject which will be open for public scrutiny.
There are also additional opportunities for public involvement in the development of exclusion and mandatory study lists, and other regulations under the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act. The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act states that the government-wide exclusion list must be developed with public input and review. This list will include projects known not to pose any risk of harm to the environment and those with negligible environmental effects. Such projects could include simple renovations, routine operations, minor construction and controlled scientific experiments. Projects on the exclusion list will not require assessment.
A mandatory study list will be compiled for projects that pose a potentially significant risk of harm to the environment. In general, these projects will tend to be large-scale projects that often generate considerable public concern. For example, large oil and gas developments, uranium mines, major hydroelectric developments and large industrial plants, could be subject to mandatory study. There will also be major opportunities for public consultation and input in the identification of other statutes and regulations that should trigger an environmental assessment under the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act.

June 27, 1990
Government Orders
The act gives authority to the Governor in Council to regulate which provisions of other federal acts will fall within this category. A preliminary review of the federal regulatory statutes suggests that some provisions of the Fisheries Act, the National Energy Board Act and the Atomic Energy Control Act may warrant being considered by the proposed legislation.
Identifying these regulatory acts in regulation, and not in the legislation itself, will provide extensive opportunity for public consultation. It will also allow the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act to remain dynamic.
Mr. Speaker, I have been talking today of the opportunities for increased and more open participation in the environmental assessment of projects. This government has, however, also introduced another major initiative that will increase public participation in the assessment of policies. For the first time ever the government is establishing a progressive environmental review process for all new policies and programs. This review process is virtually unique in the world. Under the new process, ministers have decided that the environmental implications of all proposed policy and program initiatives must be considered before decisions are taken.
The government has decided that a statement of the environmental implications of each policy and program will be released when the new policy or program is announced. Canadians will be invited at that time to scrutinize these public statements. A further opportunity for public scrutiny exists. The House of Commons Standing Committee on the Environment can request any minister to appear before it to explain the environmental implications of any new policy or program.
I remind the hon. members that this legislation is the product of considerable public consultation. The Canadian Environmental Assessment Act reflects closely the views and recommendations of Canadians gathered over the past two years on country-wide consultations.

I encourage these and other Canadians to make their views known to the House of Commons committee when it studies the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act later this year.

I think we should put the question into perspective and talk a little bit about some of the advances that have been made over the last 18 years or so.

Some of that progress has been made, and more will be made, through co-operation with the Indian people and the Inuit people themselves. In fact, Mr. Yalden pointed out in his own report that significant improvements have been made over the past several years.

Adjournment Debate
Our government is absolutely committed to strengthening the capacity of Indian peoples to provide their own government and to design systems that will be flexible to serve the needs of the communities that we are dealing with-programs that are really designed to meet the individual needs of the Indian and Inuit people who are involved, rather than quite as bureaucratic as has been perhaps in the past.
Steady progress has been achieved in transferring control of program expenditures to Indians over the past 18 years as I have mentioned. For example, in 1971, Indians managed only 20 per cent of the budgets that were set aside for their use. In 1990-1991, Indians will manage over 72 per cent of these budgets and that counts for over $1 billion in their hands for the delivery of services to Indian and Inuit peoples across the country.
Substantial progress is also being made in other areas. For example, in education, only 53 band-operated schools existed in 1975, but some five times more than that number, 280, existed last year in 1989. Enrolment in post-secondary education in 1989 had increased over 35 per cent from 1985. Contrary to interpretations that were put upon this in the report, post-secondary education budgets were actually increased very significantly to $149 million.
In the area of child welfare, there is no question that there is a need for improvement and that has been recognized. Therefore, in co-operation with Indian leadership, the federal government has entered into arrangements whereby Indian-operated child welfare agencies provide child and family services for many Indian communities. These are agencies operated by the people themselves.
Economic self-sufficiency for aboriginal people is also a priority. It is a priority for the government. This is evidenced by the establishment of the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy, or CAEDS as it is more commonly known. This strategy is a very positive initiative aimed at helping Indian and Inuit people to build their own economic structure.
In collaboration with Indian people, changes to the Indian Act are being considered. Through the lands, revenues and trust review, there is collaboration that will bring about changes that will recognize Indian authority over their own lands and money and the governance of these.
Another priority is the development of community-based self-government. The objectives of this initiative are to enhance community control and decision making and to recognize all those diverse needs and traditions that are there. Currently eight projects involving 30 bands are in negotiations. Fifteen projects involving 29 bands are working more closely toward framework agreements and over 100 bands are at the initial state of defining what community development and government means to them.
I know there is a long way to go on the issues that the hon. member mentioned, but the government is committed to achieving those goals and with co-operation and collaboration we will do so.

I was interested in a statement made earlier today by the member for Nunat-siaq, discussing what actually happens during a land claim. When the Prime Minister was making his speech, he indicated that land was being given to the Indians. In fact, when a land claim is settled Canada takes land from the Indians, gives them a bit of the remnant over which they have control and compensates them for the balance. So Canada is always the greatest beneficiary in a land claim settlement, or what the Prime Minister referred to as a modem treaty. Canada reaps the greatest benefit.
I would also like to point out that if you read the details of the framework agreement of the treaty for the Council of Yukon Indians, you will find that over the ten-year period that the Indians have agreed to take compensation, they have also agreed to phase out all of the exemptions from taxes that they enjoyed as a result of the previous arrangement they had with the federal government when the land claims were unsettled. By settling land claims you are giving an opportunity for people who have lived in those areas from 8,000 to 13,000 years and are unlikely ever to move away, to spend that capital in the area in which they live so that it has the effect of recapitalizing areas that were previously discapitalized under the old system of Canadian economics.

Mr. Speaker, as is the procedure in the late show, I will respond to the question that was referred for further debate. That is the question of the silver hake box, which as you know, Mr. Speaker, is really a small mesh gear area where all small mesh gear fishing takes place with the exception of redfish and shrimp. Fishing activities restricted to this area include silver hake, squid, and argentine.
The silver hake box was identified in the 1970s as an area where the use of small mesh gear would have minimal effect on traditional groundfish and pelagic fisheries. This zone lies approximately 100 miles off the coast of Nova Scotia and includes an area stretching from east of Sable Island to the Fundian Channel and from the edge of the Continental Shelf to the 200-mile boundary.
The silver hake has been harvested in 1990 by foreign vessels from the Soviet Union, Cuba, Japan, and Bulgaria.
By-catches of cod, haddock, and pollock are minimal in the silver hake fishery. In 1989, these amounted to 3,300 tonnes of which 2,400 tonnes was pollock. As part of the 1990 bilaterals with Cuba and the Soviet Union, negotiations have been ongoing. To date, several hundred tonnes of by-catch have been landed by U.S.S.R. vessels for Canadian processing.
Canadian fishing activities were approved for 1990. These were confined to inshore operations less than 65 feet. As well, a successful experimental fishery on Emerald Basin using MG vessels less than 65 feet has been completed.
With the exception of the inshore Emerald Basin experimental fishery, all fishing activities are within the small mesh gear zone, commonly referred to as the silver
October 1, 1990

hake box. This area does not overlap the haddock nursery closure area on Emerald and Western Bank and therefore there are no foreign activities in areas closed to Canadians.
The silver hake fishery is prosecuted in deep water on the edge of the Continental Shelf and therefore damaging to productive fishing habitat is minimal. Canadian observers are on board all foreign vessels and monitor all fishing activities.
The haddock nursery area was introduced in 1987 in an attempt to protect the excessive harvest of juvenile haddock by otter trawl vessels. The closure is landward of the silver hake box and covers an area of 5,000 square miles on Emerald and Western Banks which lie to the west of Sable Island. Mr. Speaker, I just want to point out that the government is very keenly aware of the difficulties facing the grains and oilseeds sector. Over the last number of years we have taken unprecedented steps to help farmers through the difficult times. I believe our record speaks for itself.
We established the Special Grains Program for the 1986-87 crops to ease the burden of low grain prices brought on by the international subsidy wars. This program paid out more than $2 billion over those two years.
Again in 1988, when farmers all across Canada were reeling from the effects of a devastating drought, we provided about $850 million to help them cope again. This year, we announced $450 million in assistance to grains and oilseeds producers.
Agreements have now been signed for approximately $435 million, or 96 per cent of that total. The remaining amount has been earmarked for the fur and horticultural industries, and to support soil conservation projects across Canada.
These initiatives I have just outlined constitute assistance for the grain and oilseeds industry totalling almost $3.5 billion. That is a significant commitment to the industry.
However, these special programs are not enough and we recognize that. Canadian farmers should not be expected to rely on government assistance packages year after year. An improved safety net system is needed to provide financial stability to the sector. A new program may be within sight. Over the last nine months proposals for a new program have been designed by the farmers and governments represented on the grains and oilseeds safety net committee. These people have recommended that these programs be implemented for the 1991-92 crop year.

These new programs, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan, called GRIP, and the Net Income Stabilization Account, called NISA, are designed to provide the stability farmers need. The committee believes the programs would be bankable. That means farmers would know in February or March their income position for the year. With that information, farmers can go to their banker and negotiate their credit needs.
The GRIP and NISA programs are designed to offer maximum benefits when taken together. The GRIP and NISA programs offer a way of achieving long-term stability which is needed in the grains and oilseeds sector. Our goal has to be long term stability. And whatever we do in the short term must be done with that in mind.
Adjournment Debate
We are aware of the cash flow problems that grains and oilseeds producers are now struggling with. That is why we have been meeting over the summer with farm groups and provincial governments to address this problem.
We know there have been many meetings held across the country and we know that the problems are there. Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with those problems.

Mr. Speaker, I probably will focus more on comments than on questions.
I want to address a couple of things that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond mentioned earlier and was not given an opportunity to respond to, despite his great admonitions that I should.
First, I refer to what my friend from Cape Breton- Highlands-Canso has said. The moving ahead of this legislation has come after considerable consultation with a great number of groups. I will just mention a few groups that DFO officials talked to: all provinces and territories, as well as a variety of advisory groups to the minister, including ARC, PARC and the Atlantic Council of Fisheries Ministers, in particular. They have supported that.
October 12, 1990

This legislation is being brought forward because of the determination of the current Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, and of his predecessor, both of whom feel very strongly that one of the important ways to address some of the inequities, not only in the legislation, but in the application of the law, is to impose higher fines and to bring in new sources of information.
Both of my colleagues has asked: What is the point of having new legislation if it cannot be enforced? Under the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program, there has been $52 million over five years in addition provided for surveillance and enforcement. Offshore patrols have been increased. Inshore patrols across the Atlantic will be increased. There will be more intensive use of DFO vessels for patrolling and enforcing the law. There is more money for increased armed boarding, a practice that I do not particularly like but sometimes is necessary, and increased funds for prosecution. Of course, I need not mention the agreement that we reached with the Americans that will hopefully ensure that people cannot come and go across borders unprotected.
Another thing that has been protected is the fact that there is no minimum fine. My colleague across the way referred to the level of fines. First, I should point out that the level of penalty is consistent. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the Hazardous Products Act, the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, the National Parks Act, the Railway Safety Act and the Canadian Agricultural Products Act all have no minimum fine. It allows leeway for the courts.
Do not forget, with triple, and in some cases five times, the amount of fine, a clear message is being sent to the judiciary that we are very serious and the the judiciary is forced to respond to that.
In terms of inshore versus offshore, very clearly this act allows penalties to be applied in all ways. There is a perception, and I understand it, that we are applying it purely to the inshore. I should point out, though, that as we increase the observer coverage on the offshore vessels, as we work more and more to avoid discards, culling and highgrading, we will see more and more charges laid in the offshore than ever in the inshore.
Government Orders
Then, the question comes: How is there corporate accountability and responsibility? This act ensures that it is not just the person aboard ship who ends up in court. Licence holders can be held liable for offences. Under the new act, officers and directors of corporations can be held accountable, which is a substantial change and an important change.
There is more to come, but I wanted to take this opportunity to comment on the remarks of both my friends from Cape Breton. I appreciate their support. Sometimes I wonder if that support is consistently there. One member says that the opposition is all for it and that it is gung ho, and another seems to be a little less sure. I hope we can depend on the support of the Liberal Party of Canada for this legislation at this time.

First of all, I was listening to my colleague for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso and some of the questions and comments that were made at the end of his speech. I was also listening to the comments made by the member for St. John's East. He was sort of questioning whether the Liberal Party would be supporting Bill C-74.

I was very surprised that we did not hear any mention today from our colleagues who sit a little farther down from me, but there are problems on the west coast as well, and some very serious problems. I was hoping to hear from them as well.

The reason we support Bill C-74 in general is that it increases the penalties and fines for persons who break the Fisheries Act. I should clarify the position of our party, and I am sure the position of everyone in this House. Hon. members here feel that fishermen are basically honest and hard working individuals. There are a few out there with whom there are problems. No doubt about it. Some are foreigners. Some of them are our own. But there are a few, a very few. It will also provide penalties and fines to anyone who fails to provide habitat information. It will require fishermen and processors to keep more detailed records.

There is a recognition that while Dr. Harris has told us that we need more information, particularly information from the inshore-not that we do not from the offshore-it is important that the way we go about it is consistent with fishermen and the needs of fishermen. There is a program that is very effective in New Brunswick which involves the use of information gathered by fishermen, where the fishermen work with fisheries officers to put the information together. I think he knows as well as I that there cannot be an efficient program if the co-operation is not there. In my own province, where I think in the past it would be fair to say that there has not been the level of co-operation that has been essential, we are beginning to see that now with fishermen and scientists getting together.
With regard to the lack of resources, I think my friend knows that one of the criticisms of the $584 million Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program as the response to the crisis that we face, is that there is too much money
October 12, 1990

in there for bureaucrats and not enough for programming.
It is like the rock and the hard place. On the one hand we get criticized because we are not putting enough programming in place and, on the other, because we do not have the resources to enforce the laws and the regulations. We are trying to find the balance between the scientists and the enforcement officers. We need money going into programming so that we can develop other species with, test new gear and that sort of thing, but an important point has been made.
As for not being tough enough on Americans, I think my friend recognizes that it is an easier place to run away to than perhaps Portugal or Spain. I think it is fair to say that we have made great progress with colleagues of my friend opposite in reducing the European overfishing which started in 1972. In the last year we have seen less overfishing than we have seen perhaps in the last eight or nine years. I think there is progress because there has been a multi-faceted approach or a multi-targeted approach in dealing with some of the problems.
One will find that more of the efforts are going offshore in terms of implementation and enforcing regulations as we move to more observers, as we change the observers' status, as we do more gear testing, as we collect more information, and as we get more co-operation between the scientists and the large companies.

In 1989 this government, in recognition of the critical importance of the variable entrance requirement, instituted variable entrance requirements as part of the law. It did not need temporary implementation every year. It was institutionalized in the law. The majority of the members of this House and I voted for that legislation in November of last year. It has been sitting down the hall since then. In 1981, when the government opposite changed the regulations on unemployment insurance by moving from

I voted for it and I expect the people down the way who are not elected or accountable to vote for it as well.

That is certainly the role that they have. We hope that will be all that is necessary. It would be unfair for me to predict the future.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated in his speech on this motion earlier in the House of Commons what actions he would take if circumstances changed that required some other more aggressive role. We certainly hope that will not happen and that a combination of the enforcement of the economic sanctions and other diplomatic efforts, can resolve this issue peacefully. I hear lots of different opinions and I am sure my hon. colleague is hearing, as I am, about the likelihood of that, but certainly every effort has to be made because the alternatives certainly, in my mind, are too horrific to think about, the loss of life, the children, and the loss of the future in that part of the world.
Coming back to the future of our own department, I am sure, as the hon. member is aware, it is a difficult time. We are dealing with several aspects. One, as I mentioned before, is that the Cold War is over and that is such welcome news. We believe the stability in Europe
Government Orders
has come about because of the strong role that NATO has played and, in effect, it has been able to deter aggression during some of those years that were more volatile than is the case now.
Canadians have played a role in that united force. It was not a large role but a significant one nevertheless, considering the size of our armed forces. We have always said that we will be there with our colleagues and there is a joint resolution through the CFE talks and, hopefully, to be acknowledged at the CSC meetings in November. Then we can see how we can reduce our participation. I hope that will come about and that, at a future time, we will be able to have a significant reduction in the number of troops in Europe.
We are faced, as a government and as a country, with a difficult financial situation. In our department, we have had to play our role in helping to deal with the deficit. We have taken not absolute reductions in some cases, but in others certainly less than had been planned for in terms of growth in defence spending over the past two years.
As the minister indicated in his speech yesterday, at this point in time our plans are based on only 5 per cent nominal growth, which really is no growth, because that is just the cost of inflation. That means that we do indeed have to be more creative. That is why we are now going through a process of looking at everything we do, at our taskings, at the number of people at the defence establishment review, and at our headquarters operations.
Certainly we recognize that, in the area of equipment, because of the long lapse which the Canadian Armed Forces had to endure, that there is really a backlog built up and we need better equipment. Therefore we are looking at ways to economize more effectively in areas of infrastructure or personnel in order to be able to redress that kind of balance.
As the hon. member is aware, we are looking at the utilization of our reserves, our militia, in more effective ways and combining the total force concept which we have brought to bear. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the speech by the hon. member for St. Boniface.
The present copyright legislation in this country consists of an act drafted in 1921, proclaimed in 1924, and subject to interpretation by the courts. Until quite recently, the legislation had never undergone substantial review. When I hear remarks about confusion, lack of vision and delays, I fully agree with the hon. member since the Liberal Party was in power at the time and, as usual, lacked vision, caused all kinds of delays, and created this confusion. This was typical of the Liberal government throughout its mandate, I may add!
During all those years of Liberal government, we saw, I might say, the birth of radio, television, photocopy machines, tape recorders, videocassette recorders, computers, satellites and various devices for information storage and retrieval. All these technologies have contributed to increasing the use of works protected by copyright.
These new technologies have to a very large extent been instrumental in creating works protected by copy-

However, these technologies also made it possible to make repeated use of protected works without obtaining permission from the copyright owner. For instance, we can easily reproduce a TV program at home by using a videocassette recorder, and it is practically impossible for copyright owners to control how the program is used. Consequently, new technologies have created a host of legal problems, some of which require solution through legislation. That is why the 1924 Copyright Act was partially amended in 1988 by Bill C-60 and by the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act.
In 1988, nine specific amendments were made to the Copyright Act. The maximum fine for criminal offences was raised from two hundred dollars to one million dollars; specific protection was extended to computer programs and moral rights were reinforced to protect the reputation of the author of a work; a public exhibition right for artistic work was created; the link between copyright and drafting was clarified; choreographic work was protected, whether or not it had a story line; and finally, the obligation to obtain a licence for the production of sound recordings was abolished and the application of royalties negotiated on the market was allowed.
Furthermore, Bill C-60 encouraged the creation of corporations for the collective administration of copyright or associations of copyright owners, and provided for regulations in this respect. These licensing bodies, based on a concept that has worked satisfactorily in the music industry for over 50 years, will now be able to operate in all copyright sectors and negotiate the granting of licences with users of works protected by copyright. In exchange for payment of reasonable royalties, they will give users quick and easy access to works protected by copyright. If the licensing body and the user cannot agree on what constitutes a fair royalty, either party may apply to the Copyright Board to fix the amount. Amendments to the Copyright Act have also expanded the jurisdiction of the Copyright Board.
As a result of the amendments to the Copyright Act under terms of the Canada-United States Free Trade Implementation Act, cable operators are required to compensate the holders of copyrights for the re-broad-

I say, unlike the member from the Conservative Party, that this institution is not working, that Parliament is not working, that there is a failure of this institution to respond to the needs of the people of this country. Our party, because of that, has established an action group to go across this country to try to get ideas from the Canadian people as to how to reform the Parliament of Canada to make it more responsible to the people of this country.
I find, for example, that a majority government in this country does not seem to work. It does not respond to the wishes of the people. In an election that is held today in terms of the issue of the day might be fiction in about two years time. We have a system in this country of responsible government which in theory is very good, but I ask the question of responsible for whom. Is it good enough to have an election every four or five years? I suggest it is not good enough to have an election every four or five years. A responsible government today is responsible not just to the people of this country but responsible in the main to the government side of the House and the majority Parliament in the House of Commons and that is not good enough.
The motion today by the member from Calgary is one on referenda. I am not sure whether or not he goes too far when he says there has to be a citizen initiated referendum that will be binding on the government as well as referenda initiated by the government itself. I think we should take a serious look at that proposition. We should debate the pros and cons to see whether or not this is one of the reforms to our parliamentary system. It is perhaps an idea that is much more popular in western Canada than it is in eastern Canada.
The Liberal and Conservative parties both put forward a spokesman from Ontario. If you look historically in this country, there have been since Confederation some 42 referenda conducted by provincial governments. Some 31 of them had been conducted in the four western provinces, three in the province of Ontario, two in the province of Quebec, and six in Atlantic Canada. Historically they have been used much more frequently in western Canada, perhaps because of the alienation or the grievance that many western Canadians feel about the central government and Parliament.
On the national level a referendum has been used on only two occasions. One of them was back in 1898 in terms of the prohibition of liquor. The other one was on conscription in 1942.
There are many recent examples as to why we must examine the effectiveness of our parliamentary system. We have, for example, a goods and services tax that most Canadians oppose strenuously but feel very helpless to do anything about because the government says it has mandate and, come hell or high water, that goes through regardless of the consequences.
We had a Meech Lake process. I supported very strongly the substantive part of Meech Lake which the members of this House know. The process of negotiation, which is not entirely the fault of this government but was inherited in many ways from the previous Liberal government, is a process that is too secretive. It is a process that is restricted to too few people. It is a process that must be opened up.
We also have in this parliamentary system of ours a Senate which is not democratically elected, a Senate where the Prime Minister can use an archaic constitutional provision, section 36 of our Constitution, and swamp the Senate with eight additional senators, something that is highly undemocratic.
On the other hand, there can be a majority in the Senate or a minority, as is now the case, that can override the wishes of the elected House. On either count, I do not think that is a proper way to go. Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate today in the debate, at second reading stage, on Bill C-78, the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act.
The time for speeches at this second reading stage is limited and because my native heritage is very important to me. I would like to focus my remarks on those aspects of the bill that hold special meaning for the aboriginal people of Canada. However, let me also be quick to add that this issue of environment is very important to the whole of my constituency.
Hon. members opposite have been very quick to find fault with the fact that Bill C-78 is a planning and consensus-building process based on the principle of self-assessment. It seems that they would prefer that every environmental assessment lead to a court enforceable edict by some all knowing and all powerful authority who would ensure that the best interests of the environment are defended against the inherent evils of development. Personally, I find this suggestion to be both naive and dangerous. It is also quite contraiy to the very principles of sustainable development.
Long before the arrival of Europeans on this continent, native communities were both self-governing and self-sustaining. First Nations lived in harmony with nature and were as one with the land, with their ancestors, with their children and their children's children. There was no room in native society for practices that could deplete the natural resources and damage the environments on which future generations would depend. In fact, politicians, academics, and so-called environmentalists who proclaim the virtues of sustainable development, but who fail utterly in their attempts to define such development in practical terms, would do well to reflect upon the lessons learned and the way of life practised by untold generations of native peoples in North America. They have always been, and are still, concerned with management between development and conservation.
October 25, 1990

If I were to listen too long to hon. members opposite,
I might have to conclude that the successful application of sustainable development in native society could only have been achieved through strong central decision making. But nothing could be further from the truth. The sustainability of native society has always been based firmly on consensus building, on a strong sense of community, on deep respect for the experience of elders, and on individual accountability for decisions and actions, in short, the very principles that I see underpinning the proposed Canadian Environmental Assessment Act.
Self-assessment and the accountability implicit in that concept tend to strike a very responsive cord with native people and with their ideas of sustainable development.
